name: Cultures of communication
intro: How culture shapes communication, direct and indirect styles, politeness and small talk, body language, online communities and different ways of thinking.
sammendrag:
## Communication is cultural

The way we communicate is shaped by our **culture**: our language, values, traditions and experiences. When people from different cultures meet – in real life or online – misunderstandings can happen, even when everyone speaks English. English is a **lingua franca**, a shared language used by people with different first languages.

## Direct and indirect communication

- In **direct** cultures, people say exactly what they mean. “No, that won't work” is normal and polite.
- In **indirect** cultures, people often hint and avoid saying no directly to protect relationships. “That might be difficult” can actually mean no.

British English is often described as quite indirect and polite. Phrases like “I'm not sure that's a good idea” can hide strong disagreement. Norwegians are often seen as direct, and may sound rude in English if they skip words like **please** and **could you**.

## Politeness and small talk

In many English-speaking countries, **small talk** – short, friendly conversation about the weather, the weekend or sports – is an important way to build relationships. “How are you?” is usually a greeting, not a real question. The expected answer is “Fine, thanks. And you?”

## Body language and personal space

Gestures, eye contact and **personal space** vary between cultures. In some cultures, long eye contact shows honesty, while in others it can seem rude. A thumbs-up is positive in many countries, but offensive in some. Online, **emojis** often replace body language – but their meaning can also vary between people and cultures.

## Virtual and real-world communities

Many young people belong to **online communities**: gaming clans, fan groups, chat servers and forums. These communities have their own **norms**, slang and rules. People from all over the world work together, compete and make friends. At the same time, anonymity can make some people act rudely, and **toxic behaviour** like harassment can occur.

Online and offline communication influence each other. Slang from games and memes spreads into everyday speech, and friendships from online communities can continue offline.

## Ways of thinking

People also have different **mindsets**: views on time (being punctual or relaxed), on **hierarchy** (how you address teachers or bosses), and on **individualism** versus **collectivism** (focus on “me” or “us”). None of these is right or wrong, but being aware of them makes communication easier.

## Being a good communicator

- Be curious and open-minded.
- Ask if you are unsure what someone means.
- Avoid **stereotypes** – every person is an individual.
- Adapt your language to the situation.

Gestures, facial expressions, posture and eye contact.

Unwritten rules for how to behave in a group.

options: A language used mainly by people who share the same first language
A language created by combining parts of several different languages
A language spoken by most people within one country
A shared language used by people with different first languages
quiz.explain: English is the most widely used lingua franca today.

quiz.text: What might “That might be difficult” mean in an indirect culture?
options: Yes, that sounds easy.
No.
I need more details first.
Let's try it right away.
quiz.explain: Indirect speakers often avoid saying no directly.

options: A short conversation about a difficult personal problem
A planned discussion about news and current events
Short, friendly conversation about everyday topics
A formal talk about work or school problems

quiz.text: How should you usually answer “How are you?” in English?
options: “Fine, thanks. And you?”
“I have had a difficult week.”
“What do you mean by that?”
“I’m not ready to talk.”
quiz.explain: The question is usually a friendly greeting.

quiz.text: Why might Norwegians sometimes sound rude in English?
options: Because they may speak too quietly for English speakers to hear them
Because they may leave out polite phrases like “please” and “could you”
Because they may use too much small talk before making a request
Because they may use indirect phrases that sound unclear to English speakers
quiz.explain: Norwegian is often more direct than English.

options: A website where people post messages about shared interests
A group of people who play one game together offline
A place where people buy and sell things online
A group of people who meet and interact online
quiz.explain: Gaming clans and fan groups are examples.

options: Harassment and rude behaviour towards others
Sharing personal opinions and helpful advice with other users
Disagreeing politely with another player in a discussion
Using strong language to complain about a game's rules
quiz.explain: Anonymity can make toxic behaviour more common.

options: A focus on personal success and individual choices
A focus on collecting shared objects in a group
A focus on the group and “us”
A focus on competition between members of a group
quiz.explain: In collectivist cultures, family and group needs often come first.

quiz.text: What can a thumbs-up mean in different cultures?
options: It is offensive in many countries, but positive in some
It means approval in many countries, but asks someone to stop in some
It is a greeting in many countries, but a warning in some
It is positive in many countries, but offensive in some
quiz.explain: Gestures do not always travel well between cultures.

quiz.text: What is a good way to avoid misunderstandings across cultures?
options: Assume the person shares your customs and communication style
Ask if you are unsure what someone means
Use stereotypes to predict how the person will respond
Keep the conversation short to reduce chances of confusion
quiz.explain: Asking shows interest and prevents mistakes.

ekstra.text: Everyone who speaks English communicates in exactly the same way.
ekstra.explain: Culture shapes how people use English.

ekstra.text: Online communities often have their own norms and slang.
ekstra.explain: New members learn these unwritten rules over time.

ekstra.text: Emojis can be understood differently by different people.
ekstra.explain: The same emoji can be friendly to one person and sarcastic to another.

ekstra.text: Direct communication is always better than indirect communication.
ekstra.explain: Both styles are normal in different cultures.

options: The area someone uses for sleeping and getting dressed
The distance people like to keep between themselves and others
The space someone controls on their online profile
The distance people stand from objects in a public place
ekstra.explain: The comfortable distance varies between cultures.

ekstra.text: Which phrase is a polite way to disagree in British English?
options: I disagree; your suggestion is completely wrong.
No, that is a terrible suggestion.
I'm not sure that's a good idea.
You have misunderstood the whole situation.
A simplified idea about a group of people
A negative judgment about one person based on their actions
A shared custom practiced by members of a group
A positive belief about one individual’s personality
ekstra.explain: Stereotypes ignore that people are individuals.

skriv.text: What is culture, and how can it shape the way people communicate?
skriv.fasit: Culture includes a group’s shared language, values, traditions and experiences. It can influence how people express themselves and understand others.
kriterier: Explains that culture includes shared features such as language, values, traditions or experiences.
Connects culture to how people communicate or understand communication.

skriv.text: Compare direct and indirect communication. How does each style express disagreement?
skriv.fasit: In direct communication, people say exactly what they mean, so they may say clearly that they disagree. In indirect communication, people may hint at disagreement or avoid saying no to protect relationships.
kriterier: Explains that direct communication states meaning clearly.
Explains that indirect communication hints or avoids a direct no, often to protect relationships.

skriv.text: You want a classmate to help you with homework. Write a polite request in English and explain what makes it polite.
skriv.fasit: Could you help me with my homework, please? “Could you” and “please” make the request sound more polite than a direct command.
kriterier: Gives a clear request using a politeness marker such as “please” or “could you”.
Explains that the marker makes the request more polite or less direct.

skriv.text: In some cultures, long eye contact can show honesty, while in others it can seem rude. Explain why the same eye contact might be understood differently.
skriv.fasit: Eye contact is part of body language, and body language varies between cultures. People can therefore interpret the same gesture in different ways.
kriterier: Identifies eye contact as body language or a non-verbal signal.
Explains that cultural differences can lead people to interpret it differently.

skriv.text: Emojis can replace body language in online messages, but their meaning can vary between people and cultures. Explain how this could lead to a misunderstanding.
skriv.fasit: A sender may use an emoji to show one meaning or feeling, while the receiver understands it differently. The message can then be misunderstood even though it includes an emoji.
kriterier: Explains that people may understand the same emoji differently.
Connects this difference in meaning to a possible misunderstanding online.

skriv.text: A gaming clan has its own slang and unwritten rules. Explain what these rules are called and what they tell members.
skriv.fasit: The unwritten rules are called norms. They tell members how people are expected to behave in the group.
kriterier: Identifies the unwritten rules as norms.
Explains that norms guide or describe how members should behave.

skriv.text: Online and offline communication can influence each other. Give one example of this and explain how the two are connected.
skriv.fasit: Slang from games or memes can spread into everyday speech. This shows that language used online can influence how people communicate offline.
kriterier: Gives a relevant example, such as online slang spreading into everyday speech or an online friendship continuing offline.
Explains how the example connects online and offline communication.

skriv.text: One student thinks it is important to be punctual, while another is more relaxed about time. Explain how their different mindsets could cause a misunderstanding, and why neither view is automatically right or wrong.
skriv.fasit: They may expect different things about when someone should arrive, so one student could misunderstand the other’s behaviour. Different views about time are mindsets, and neither is automatically right or wrong.
kriterier: Explains how different expectations about time could cause a misunderstanding.
Recognises that different mindsets are not automatically right or wrong.
